content.title: This paper introduces a novel meta-learning framework with the attention-on-label mechanism for efficient learning from multiple sets of noisy annotators. The proposed network can learn, from both the image and its associated text, to predict the class membership through a weighted summation of individual noisy annotators. Comparisons with different methods on several datasets show that the proposed framework can lead to improvement in predictive accuracy.
content.review:
Pros.

    • The proposed training framework can calculate the image labels on-the-fly with an attention-on-label scheme.

    • Gradient flows toward labels are employed to optimize the attention-on-label parameters.

    • The performance of the proposed methodology is demonstrated through experiments on several datasets.


Cons.

    • While the idea of learning from multiple annotations can prove to be useful, the rationale of learning from multiple noisy and automatically generated labels needs further justification since the model can only be as successful as the best algorithm by which the labels are generated; hence, instead of learning from the knowledge of human expert annotators, only an already known function is being estimated.

    • The simulations can be improved for a more rigorous illustration of the method’s benefits. Simulations show marginal improvement over very common and baseline methods such as ResNet-50 network.

    • Since the main novelty of the paper lies within learning an attention on the labels, it would be more appropriate if the comparison is made with other attention-based methods instead of baseline methods; however, those experiments are missing.

    • There is a typo in the word "globla" in the line before Eq. (4).
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

display_title: Our method outperforms the baseline and the SOTA with a large margin.

content.title: Our method outperforms the baseline and the SOTA with a large margin.
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments.

Responses to the comments:
1. As we stated at the very end of Experiments Section, "our proposed method actually achieves higher or similar accuracy in comparison to the NLP annotators while a model trained with NLP mined labels usually can not reach the same level of accuracy as the labels themselves, e.g., R50 is trained with negbio_u1". The reviewer is right about "since the model can only be as successful as the best algorithm". The proposed method is about learning the best from the available annotation sets and make the model achieve similar accuracy as the best annotation itself, which is already an attractive feature for the training process. We can further observe this in Figure 5 of the Appendix when the proposed method can achieve similar results as the model trained with the best label set (HS) across different noise levels. 

2. As shown in Table 2-4 and Figures in Appendix, the proposed method outperforms the baseline with a large margin, i.e., 14% over baseline (trained with AVG) and 8% over SOTA on CIFAR, and 4% over the baseline and 2% over the SOTA on hand-labeled OpenI chest x-ray data (trained with data of noise level of 15-20%).  

3. As mentioned in the method section, other attention methods are not competitors but components could be utilized to replace the simplest soft-max-based attention method we have right now. I am not sure how other attention methods can be adopted here without the meta training part. Indeed, it might be a good ablation study to see how different attention module can help with the final performance. In addition to proving the concept as we did here, we will try to integrate other attention mechanisms in the future manuscript, e.g., including the self-attention module to achieve a better F_m.

content.title: Novel approach; would be great to benchmark this technique against more baselines
content.review:
In this paper, the authors propose a meta-training technique to work with image datasets with multiple noisy-label sets. I read this paper with great interest; this is a novel framework that is definitely worth exploring.

I have a few questions and concerns that I’m hoping that the authors can help me with:
1. Given multiple noisy label sets, it will be ideal if we can compare and benchmark your technique to: (1) majority vote: for every image, assign the label that appears in the majority of the noisy labels, and then train the image model using majority vote labels (2) assigning weights to noisy label sets based on how frequently they agree with the majority. For e.g. for the chest x-ray classification task where you have 4 labels sets: chexpert_u0, chexpert_u1, negbio_u0, and negbio_u1, let’s assign an overall weight to chexpert_u0 based on how many times chexpert_u0 agrees with the majority of the 4 label sets; similarly, let’s assign an overall weight to chexpert_u1, negbio_u0, negbio_u1. Now, let’s normalize the weights. For each image, the “final” label is the weighted sum over the label sets.
2. I’m not fully convinced that “average y_bar = [] are in the range of [0, 1], which is rather ambiguous for the model to learn. Binarization will be useful to cast the value close to either 0 or 1”.  The range gives an insight into the “confidence” of the label. You can also discard images with labels that fall in the [0.45-0.55] range. Did you do this because there will be a lot of labels in the [0.45-0.55] range in the initial iterations of training?
3. I’d make it explicit that you got labels for OpenI using negbio_u[0,1] and chexpert_u[0,1]. I was initially confused where you got multiple label sets for OpenI from, given that OpenI comes with hand labels and table 3 says OpenI (hand-labeled). I only cleared my confusion by reading the appendix.

I’m supportive of accepting this paper; it would be great if we can get the techniques benchmarked against more baselines (as I mentioned in 1).
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Thank you for the detailed comments. Questions answered.
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the detailed comments and the time devoted to it.

Responses to your questions:
1. We agree these two are decent baselines to compare with. We did a quick experiment on the first one, i.e., majority vote (MV). Results on MIMIC-CXR 1K hand-labeled data are shown below. In all, it has a similar performance as R50 (trained with negbio_u1, one of the label sets). We believe it will work better in a scenario when one of the labelers has serious errors and the majority voting can cancel out such influence. We will post further experimental results in the future manuscript.

Image-only; R50; MV; CM; Ours

AVG AUCs; 0.732; 0.737; 0.736; 0.755

Image-text; R50; MV; CM; Ours

AVG AUCs; 0.842; 0.837; 0.837; 0.868 

2. The dividing point of binarization is controlled by T. we experimented with different values and find the current setting with T=0.5 and k=50 provide the best results. 
3. As we state for the OpenI in the Datasets section, "To keep the consistency with MIMIC-CXR dataset, we use the same 14 categories of findings as mentioned above in the experiments." The category of hand-labeled labels from OpenI is more than the ones in MIMIC-CXR, we only utilized the ones consistent with MIMIC-CXR. We will make it clear in the future manuscript.

content.title: Recommend to reject
content.review:
The authors introduce an attention-based method for learning with noisy labels using multiple labelers based on learning a meta-model to provide attentional weighting of the labels. They compare their method against that of (Tanno et al., Learning From Noisy Labels By Regularized Estimation Of Annotator Confusion, 2019) and (Zhang et. al., "When radiology report generation meets knowledge graph", 2019) on CIFAR10 and chest x-ray datasets. 

I found the explanation of the method somewhat confusing. Overall, this appears to be a more complex method than Tanno et al.'s, and with limited improvement. Unconvincingly, in fact, it appears that the proposed method does not perform as well as any of the other methods compared including the baseline ResNet 50 on the MIMIC-CXR dataset, and not as well as Zhang et al.'s method (labeled NG) on OpenI dataset. 

Minor errors:

Uneven number of parenthesis in equation 2. 
Typo: "with the attended label and a globla learning rate"
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper

display_title: Hope the reviewer can provide more details to help improve the submission

content.title: Hope the reviewer can provide more details to help improve the submission
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments.

1. We will really appreciate it if the reviewer could provide more details about the confusion you have when going through the proposed method. Many thanks! 
The proposed algorithm is fairly easy to adopt (Please see the pseudo-code we provided in the Appendix). 

2. In section 5.3, we explained the reason that our results "look" worse than others in MIMIC-CXR with "NLP-mined" labels as follows:
"The averaged AUC for Ours actually drops from the baseline. Considering the fact that the testing set of MIMIC-CXR dataset
is also using the algorithm based labels, our predictions actually diverge from those noisy labels and lean to the underlying true labels. It is proved by the results illustrated in OpenI dataset section (right part of Table 3)."

Our intention here is to show the results for better insights into how the NLP-mined labels could influence both the training and the testing. However, it has caused confusion for the reviewer. We will remove them and replace them with evaluation on hand-labeled data only, which are already included in the current manuscript. On both the 1K MIMIC-CXR hand-labeled data and OpenI (which is also hand-labeled), our method has demonstrated superior results in comparison to previous works and the state-of-the-art method (Tanno et al. 2019)
